title: Mata Khivi, named in the Granth
hookLine: Guru Angad's wife is praised by name in the minstrels' Var for her generous kitchen (Ramkali, ang 967)

lines: A HUGE POT OF RICE PUDDING.
cards: A huge pot of rice pudding, thick and sweet, a ladle as long as a forearm, and a line of people that doesn't end. Somebody has to decide the pudding gets real ghee, not the cheap stuff, even with so many mouths.
That somebody, in the Guru's house at Khadur, has a name, and the name made it into scripture. It's also the end of a week, so there's a look back too.

teach.b: Mata Khivi was the wife of Guru Angad, and Sikhs remember her as the one who ran the langar, the free kitchen, at Khadur. Some people in this part of the path are known mainly from later stories, like the janamsakhis.
Mata Khivi is named in the Granth itself. Remember Satta and Balvand, the minstrels whose Var sits in Raag Ramkali? On Ang 967, Balvand speaks of her.

teach.h: SHADE LIKE A LEAFY TREE; KHEER WITH GHEE.
teach.b: In paraphrase: Khivi is a good woman, and her shade is thick and cool, like a leafy tree. In the langar, the wealth of the Word is shared out, and rice pudding made with ghee is served, sweet as nectar.
Two kinds of food in one line: the Word, given freely, and kheer, rice pudding rich with ghee, given just as freely. Shade is the picture: people come in from the heat and rest under her care.

A woman's kitchen work is honored in the Guru's book, by name, as part of the Guru's house. The langar isn't a side room to the faith; it's where the faith gets fed to people. And the generosity is in the ghee.
Feeding many people cheaply would have been easier. The line praises richness.

teach.h: A WEEK OF VOICES AND A HOME.
teach.b: Now the week: which voice speaks to you. One Guru, many voices. The Bhagats close, with room for all.
Then home: Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu, love and worry. Bebe Nanaki and Jai Ram, family who helps. Mata Sulakhni, steady at home.
And today, Mata Khivi's generous kitchen.

how: Gurdwaras run a langar, a free kitchen where anyone may sit and eat, and Sikhs remember Mata Khivi as one who shaped that service at Khadur Sahib.

o: a Bhagat whose hymns praise the kitchen
a cook paid to feed the Guru's guests
Guru Angad's wife, who ran the langar

games.q: Mata Khivi's kitchen — tap the pairs.
p: thick and cool, like a leafy tree

s: Mata Khivi is known only from later stories
she's named in the Granth itself, in the Var of Satta and Balvand on Ang 967.
the Var says the langar shares the wealth of the Word
the Word and the rice pudding are both given freely.
the line praises feeding people as cheaply as possible
it praises kheer made rich with ghee.

games.q: you're running the langar and the line of hungry people is long. ghee is expensive. what do you do?
o: use less ghee so the pudding stretches.
serve only the first part of the line.
make the kheer rich with ghee for everyone.
games.why: Balvand's line praises Mata Khivi's langar for kheer made with ghee, sweet as nectar.

practice: Picture a meal you'll make or share this week, and who could eat it with you.

Then picture the ghee: the one thing you could make a little richer than you have to, more of something good, a second helping set aside, a neighbor's plate. If you pray, you can breathe Waheguru out with it.

wordCard.voice: Mata Khivi. Guru Angad's wife, who ran the langar at Khadur and is praised by name in the Var of Satta and Balvand, her kitchen serving kheer made with ghee.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: langar, the free kitchen of the Guru's house.

carryVoice: Your line: generous kitchen. Cool shade for everyone, and real ghee in the pot. That's the week.

sources.ref: Ramkali ki Var, Satta and Balvand, Ang 967
